scenario.title: Three yields, one number
scenario.intro: Three projects report yield for the same institutional KPI. In Kenya a maize team runs crop cuts on farmers' plots. In Ethiopia a trial team harvests net plots under a station protocol. In South Asia a wheat team estimates yield from a regional model built on trial and farm data. All three report tons per hectare. Now the annual KPI run needs one institutional figure, and someone has to produce it without pretending the three numbers are the same thing. This module shows you how the Toolbox makes that possible.

objectives.text: Describe the KPI Toolbox: 142 indicators in 13 volumes, ten impact and three enabling pathways, the three Thrusts, and the cross-cutting role of Volume 1.
Explain why one KPI can have several valid measurement levels and methods, and what harmonisation does and does not require.

Apply the aggregation rule: recompute institutional values from eligible records with the indicator's method and report them with coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality, never as an unqualified sum of project totals.
Distinguish setting a local scope from silently redefining an institutional KPI, and route proposed KPI changes through MEAL review.
Read a KPI reference sheet, name the fields it defines, and interpret a quality rating the way a reviewer would.
Connect observation-level data to a decision-relevant question and explain why a sum of reported numbers cannot answer what CIMMYT contributed to yield change in Kenya.

lessons.title: One KPI, many valid methods: the yield example

beats.hook: Crop cuts in Kenya, net-plot harvests in Ethiopia, a regional model in South Asia. Same KPI, three methods. Is that a problem, or is that the design?

example.title: Three teams, one yield KPI
body: The Kenyan maize team measures at farm and plot level. The reference sheet lets them choose direct measurement, crop cuts or a farmer survey. The standard is to use the most reliable method feasible in context, document the method used and assign a quality rating. They choose crop cuts on sampled plots, record that choice, and their records carry a rating in the high-to-medium range that the farm level allows.

The Ethiopian trial team measures at trial and station level. Here the standards are tighter: yield is measured on the net plot, adjusted to a standard moisture (the framework's example is 12.5% for maize), with a minimum plot size and number of repetitions. Controlled protocols earn a high rating.

The South Asian wheat team works at region and country level. Their figure is aggregated from multiple trials and farm records, with modelling or spatial interpolation where needed. Their standards are to define inclusion criteria, weight by area or representativeness, and report uncertainty bounds. The rating is variable, so they document coverage and method quality.

None of the three is doing it wrong. Harmonisation does not require every project to measure the same thing in the same way. It requires that, when they measure the same concept, they share a definition, a methodological logic and rules that allow interpretation and, where valid, aggregation. The yield KPI gives each team the method suited to the decision at hand, and the rules for bringing the results together.

bullets: A common KPI does not imply one method everywhere. Each measurement level has its own valid methods, key standards and quality rating.
Harmonisation means a shared definition, methodological logic and interpretation rules, not identical instruments.
Document the method and the rating with every record. That is what lets the levels reconverge later.

lessons.title: Aggregation: from plots to institutional totals without double counting

beats.hook: Three project figures sit in a spreadsheet. The quickest institutional number is the sum. It is also the one number the framework forbids.

example.title: Allowed or not allowed?
example.prompt: Section 3.3 sets how institutional values are produced. Sort each practice into allowed or not allowed.

bins.label: Allowed under 3.3
bins.hint: Recomputed from eligible records with the indicator's method, reported with its qualifiers.

bins.label: Not allowed
bins.hint: Shortcuts that lose eligibility, overlap, weighting or uncertainty.

cards.label: De-duplicate farmers who appear in two projects' lists using persistent identifiers
cards.why: De-duplication is one of the methods section 3.3 names, and persistent identifiers exist to prevent double counting.

cards.label: Weight farm records by area or representativeness before combining them
cards.why: Weighting is a named aggregation method, and the regional yield standard says to weight by area or representativeness.

cards.label: Add the three project yield figures and report the sum as the institutional value
cards.why: An unqualified sum of project totals is exactly what the framework rules out.

cards.label: Pool the eligible microdata and recompute with the indicator's method
cards.why: Institutional values are recomputed from eligible underlying records. Pooling microdata is a named method.

cards.label: Average the three project figures without checking units or populations
cards.why: An average of totals is still a shortcut over the records. It ignores eligibility, weighting and overlap.

cards.label: Report the value with its coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality
cards.why: These four qualifiers travel with every institutional result.

cards.label: Drop the uncertainty bound so the dashboard shows one clean number
cards.why: Uncertainty is part of the reported result, not an optional footnote.

cards.label: Triangulate with compatible secondary sources under documented rules
cards.why: Triangulation with compatible secondary sources is listed in 3.3, subject to the triangulation rule in 2.6.

cards.label: Include records whose method was never documented, to raise coverage
cards.why: Only eligible records enter the calculation. A record without a documented method cannot be rated or judged eligible.

cards.label: Roll the recomputed results up by KPI volume and then by Thrust
cards.why: That is the roll-up order section 3.3 describes.

bullets: Institutional values are recomputed from eligible underlying records using the method defined for the indicator.
Depending on the KPI that may mean de-duplication, weighting, pooling, extrapolation, spatial interpolation, modelling, meta-analysis or triangulation.
The result carries coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality. It is never an unqualified sum of project totals.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

beats.hook: The Kenyan team only works on irrigated plots in two counties. The investor wants seed recipients counted as adopters. One of these is fine. One of these is not.

example.title: Scope you may set, meaning you may not change
body: Local scope. The Kenyan maize team applies the institutional yield KPI to irrigated plots in two counties, in the main season only. It writes that scope into its measurement plan and its crosswalk. The concept, unit of observation, valid method and calculation rule are untouched. When the KPI engine recomputes the institutional value, the Kenyan records enter with their scope attached. That is what section 3.2 allows: projects may specify their local scope.

Silent redefinition. The same team's investor template counts any farmer who received seed as an adopter. If the team quietly reports seed recipients under the institutional adoption KPI label, the meaning of the indicator has changed while its name has not. Anyone combining it with other projects' adoption records will be adding two different things. That is what 3.2 forbids: projects do not silently redefine the institutional indicator.
The right move is the one you met in the crosswalk lesson. Keep the institutional definition. Report the investor measure separately from the same registry, with the difference noted.

And if a team believes the institutional definition itself is wrong for its context? Governance rule 1 in section 5.3 applies. No existing KPI is redefined, and no new institutional KPI is added, without review by the MEAL team. Projects can add project-specific indicators, but these are not reported as institutional KPIs until the Design, Standards & Enablement pillar has reviewed and approved them. Approved changes are published in a new version of the MEAL Handbook. A label in a dashboard is not an approval.

bullets: Local scope says where and for whom the KPI applies in your project. It leaves the concept, unit, method and calculation intact.
Silent redefinition changes what the indicator means while keeping its label. It breaks comparability across projects.
Changes to an institutional KPI go through MEAL review and a new Handbook version. Project-specific indicators stay project-specific until approved.

source.title: Governance

beats.hook: A KPI name and a target tell you what to report. The reference sheet tells you how to measure it so that the number can be trusted and combined.

example.title: Nine things the sheet defines, and what you do with each
body: For every KPI, CIMMYT defines the concept, the unit of observation, the data sources, the valid methods by measurement level, the calculation and aggregation rules, the disaggregation, the quality assurance requirements and the data provenance. Each volume of the Toolbox contains full reference sheets. The course does not reproduce the 142 sheets, so this lesson teaches you how to read one, not what any particular sheet says.

When the Kenyan Focal Point writes the measurement plan row for yield, the sheet supplies most of the answers. Unit of observation: from the sheet. Source and valid method: from the valid methods by measurement level, choosing the farm and plot row. Disaggregation: from the sheet. What the project adds is its local scope, its frequency, its coverage, its owner and its timing.

When a Regional MEAL Lead reviews that row, the sheet is the checklist. Is the method one the sheet lists for that level? Does the plan meet the key standards for that level? Will the records carry the disaggregation and provenance the sheet requires, so the central recomputation can use them?

When the data system builds a form, it builds it from the reference sheet too. That is why section 4.1 says forms are built from the KPI reference sheets. Sheet, plan row, form and KPI engine all read from the same definition. Change the sheet and everything downstream changes with it, which is why a redefinition needs MEAL review.

bullets: A reference sheet defines concept, unit of observation, data sources, valid methods by level, calculation and aggregation rules, disaggregation, quality assurance requirements and provenance.
The sheet supplies the fixed parts of a measurement plan row. The project adds scope, frequency, coverage, owner and timing.
Forms, plan rows and the KPI engine all read from the same sheet. That is what makes evidence comparable and reusable.

lessons.title: Quality ratings and what they tell a reviewer

beats.hook: Two yield records, both in tons per hectare, both from Kenya. One came from a crop cut, one from a farmer's recollection. The rating is how the difference survives into the database.

example.title: Three ratings, one regional estimate
body: The yield example in section 3.2 gives each measurement level a rating band. Farm and plot: high to medium, depending on the method. Trial and station: high, because of controlled protocols. Region and country: variable, so coverage and method quality must be documented.

A reviewer reads the rating as a statement about reliability given the method, not as a grade for the team. A medium rating on a farmer survey is an honest record. A missing rating is the problem, because a record with no documented method cannot be judged eligible, weighted sensibly or interpreted later.

When the South Asian wheat team builds its regional estimate from high-rated trial records and medium-rated farm records, the estimate does not inherit the best rating in the set, and it does not throw the farm records away. It documents its coverage and method quality, and each underlying record keeps its own method and rating, so the figure can be recalculated when methods improve.

The standard at farm level is the most reliable method feasible in context. Feasible is doing real work in that sentence. A crop cut on every plot in a county may not be feasible. A documented, rated survey is better than an undocumented crop cut.

bullets: Farm and plot methods rate high to medium depending on method. Trial protocols rate high. Regional estimates are variable and must document coverage and method quality.
A rating describes reliability given the method. Record the method and the rating with every observation.
Aggregates do not inherit the best rating in the set. Each record keeps its own rating so the figure can be recalculated.

lessons.title: From observation-level data to decision-relevant insight

beats.hook: Leadership asks a simple question: what has CIMMYT contributed to yield change in Kenya? Three project totals cannot answer it. Here is what can.

example.title: The Kenya yield question
body: Section 3.3 uses this exact question as its example. Answering it needs contribution or attribution analysis against a credible counterfactual, agronomic, socioeconomic and climate modelling, adoption data and geospatial assessment. A sum of reported numbers cannot answer it.

Look at what each ingredient needs. A counterfactual needs plot and farm records with identifiers, so adopters can be compared with non-adopters. Climate modelling needs the records to carry location and season. Adoption data need the participant registry linked to later observations. Geospatial assessment needs ground records to calibrate against. Every ingredient is observation-level data, kept with its provenance.

That is why institutional values are recomputed from eligible underlying records rather than compiled from project reports. Records can be disaggregated, re-analysed, audited and recalculated as methods improve. Totals cannot. The data system keeps the records and their provenance for that reason.

The three project yield figures from the scenario are still useful. Each one tells its own project something about its own plots. What they cannot do, added or averaged, is answer the institutional question. The framework builds the answer from the records underneath them.

bullets: The Kenya yield question needs contribution or attribution analysis against a credible counterfactual, modelling, adoption data and geospatial assessment.
Every one of those ingredients is observation-level data with provenance. A sum of reported numbers cannot answer the question.
Recomputing from records lets results be disaggregated, audited and recalculated. That is the path from data to decision-relevant insight.

frames.narration: The yield KPI fans out into three measurement levels. At farm and plot level: direct measurement, crop cuts or a farmer survey. At trial and station level: harvested-plot measurement under standard protocols. At region and country level: aggregation from trials and farm data, with modelling where needed.

frames.narration: Each level has its own key standards. Farm: most reliable method feasible, documented and rated. Trial: net plot, standard moisture, minimum plot size and repetitions. Region: inclusion criteria, weighting, uncertainty bounds.

items.label: Farm / plot
items.detail: Most reliable feasible method. Document and rate.

items.label: Trial / station
items.detail: Net plot. Standard moisture. Plot size and repetitions.

frames.narration: Take one trial standard. A fresh harvest weighs more than a dry one. So the protocol measures the net plot and adjusts the yield to a standard moisture. The framework's example for maize is 12.5 percent. Only after that dial completes are two trials comparable.
This is what harmonisation means. What is shared: the definition, the methodological logic and the interpretation rules. What varies by level: the method, the key standards and the quality rating.

Now the three levels reconverge. The KPI engine recomputes from the eligible records with the indicator's method. What comes out is one value, and it never travels alone: coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality travel with it. The figures here are an illustration.

scene.note: Provenance and method quality recorded. Illustrative figures.

frames.narration: Projects may set their local scope. They do not silently redefine the institutional indicator. That one sentence is what makes the fan close again.

scene.title: Local scope, yes. Silent redefinition, no.
scene.subtitle: Shared definition and rules let three methods become one value.

frames.narration: The method depends on the KPI. Section 3.3 lists what it may involve: de-duplication, weighting, pooling of microdata, extrapolation, spatial interpolation, modelling or meta-analysis, and triangulation with compatible secondary sources.
What comes out is a value with four companions: coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality. Then results roll up by KPI volume and by Thrust. Never an unqualified sum of project totals.

scene.note: Provenance and method quality attached. Rolled up by volume, then Thrust.

Governance rule 1: the MEAL team reviews, the Design, Standards and Enablement pillar approves, and the change is published in a new version of the Handbook. Until then, a project-specific indicator stays project-specific.
Keep the institutional definition. Report the investor measure separately. Write your scope down. Ask for review when the definition itself must change.

frames.narration: For every KPI, CIMMYT defines nine things. The concept. The unit of observation. The data sources. The valid methods by measurement level. The calculation and aggregation rules. The disaggregation. The quality assurance requirements. The data provenance.

The methods section reads like a table. One row per measurement level. For yield: farm and plot, trial and station, region and country. Each row names the method, the key standards and the quality rating. Your measurement plan row picks one level and follows that row.
Forms are built from the sheet. Plan rows are checked against it. The KPI engine computes with it. Read the sheet before you plan, and you will not be surprised at the annual run.

scene.title: Read the sheet before you plan the row
scene.subtitle: Sheet, form, plan row and engine share one definition.

frames.narration: A quality rating says how reliable a measurement is, given the method used. Farm-level methods earn high to medium, depending on the method. Trial protocols earn high. An undocumented method earns nothing, because nobody can rate it.
Three levels, three rating bands. Farm and plot: high to medium. Trial and station: high, controlled protocols. Region and country: variable, so document coverage and method quality.

scene.gap: Same number. Only A is usable.

frames.narration: Ratings travel with the record. An aggregate does not inherit the best one in the set. It documents its own coverage and method quality.

scene.title: The rating travels with the record
scene.subtitle: Document the method. Assign the rating. Keep both.

frames.narration: The question the framework uses as its own example: what has CIMMYT contributed to yield change in Kenya?

scene.title: What has CIMMYT contributed to yield change in Kenya?
scene.subtitle: The framework's own example question.

frames.narration: Three project reports cannot answer it. So the framework dissolves the reports into the observations underneath: plots, trials, farms, participants, each with identifiers and provenance.

Answering needs four things the records make possible. Contribution or attribution analysis against a credible counterfactual. Agronomic, socioeconomic and climate modelling. Adoption data. Geospatial assessment. A sum of reported numbers cannot provide any of them.

From records to decision. Eligible records go into the KPI engine. Out comes a value with coverage, uncertainty, provenance and method quality. It rolls up by volume and Thrust, and leadership gets an answer it can act on and audit.

misconceptions.description: You added or averaged project totals to get an institutional figure. The framework recomputes from eligible records with the indicator's method and never reports an unqualified sum of project totals.

You assumed that a shared KPI means every project must use the identical method. A common KPI has valid methods for each measurement level; harmonisation shares the definition and rules, not the instrument.

You changed what an institutional indicator means to fit a local activity or an investor template while keeping its label. Projects set local scope; redefinition needs MEAL review and a new Handbook version.
You treated two figures with the same name or unit as comparable without checking that they share a definition, a methodological logic and the rules for interpretation and aggregation.
You combined or compared records without recording the method and its quality rating, or you let an aggregate borrow the best rating in the set. Each record keeps its method and rating.
You mixed up the Toolbox's parts: volumes, Thrusts, impact and enabling pathways. Impact volumes sit under three Thrusts; enabling volumes are reported alongside them; Volume 1 is cross-cutting.

questions.explanation: Farm-level methods rate high to medium depending on the method, and the rating records that difference so later analysis can weight or interpret the records appropriately. Documentation makes a record usable; it does not make every method equally reliable.

questions.question: Leadership asks: what has CIMMYT contributed to yield change in Kenya? Which answer does the framework give?

options.text: Sum the yield figures reported by every project working in Kenya
Report the average of trial yields across all Kenyan stations
Quote the number of farmers reached with improved varieties
Run contribution analysis against a counterfactual, with modelling, adoption and geospatial data

questions.explanation: Section 3.3 uses this question as its example and says it needs contribution or attribution analysis against a credible counterfactual, modelling, adoption data and geospatial assessment. A sum of reported numbers cannot answer it.

questions.question: A regional report lists Volume 11, Institutional performance and operations, under the Peace Thrust. What is wrong?

Volume 11 belongs under Human Wellbeing rather than under Peace
Nothing is wrong. Every one of the 13 volumes sits under one Thrust
Volume 11 is cross-cutting, so it belongs under all three Thrusts at once

questions.explanation: Volumes 11, 12 and 13 are enabling pathways that measure how CIMMYT itself performs, and they are reported alongside the Thrusts, not under one. Only Volume 1 is cross-cutting.

The KPI volume

The investor portfolio

questions.question: Three projects report the same institutional yield KPI: crop cuts in Kenya, trial protocols in Ethiopia, a regional model in South Asia. A manager insists that all three switch to crop cuts before the figures can be used. What does the framework say?

options.text: The manager is right. Harmonisation requires one method everywhere.
A common KPI does not imply one method everywhere. Each level has its own valid methods.
Only the trial protocol is valid, so the other two figures must be dropped.
The regional model should replace the other two because it covers more area.

questions.explanation: Section 3.2 opens with the statement that a common KPI does not imply one method everywhere, and gives yield three measurement levels with different valid methods. Forcing one method would discard fit-for-purpose evidence, not harmonise it.

questions.question: Which key standards does the yield example set for the Region / Country measurement level?

options.text: Measure on the net plot, adjust to standard moisture, meet the minimum plot size
Apply the trial protocol to every farm across the whole region
Collect every available yield number and report the total area covered
Define inclusion criteria, weight by area or representativeness, report uncertainty bounds

questions.question: Three projects in Kenya, Ethiopia and Zambia each submit a yield figure for the same institutional KPI. The annual run must produce one institutional value. What does the KPI engine do?

options.text: Recompute from the eligible underlying records using the method the indicator defines
Add the three figures and report the total as the institutional yield
Average the three figures, since each one is already an approved KPI value
Report the Kenyan figure alone because it rests on the most plots

questions.explanation: Institutional values are recomputed from eligible underlying records using the method defined for the indicator, and the KPI engine exists to replace summing project reports. Averaging totals is still a shortcut over the records.

options.text: Spatial interpolation
Extrapolation
De-duplication
Meta-analysis

questions.explanation: De-duplication removes the same person counted twice, and persistent identifiers exist so this can be done across projects. Interpolation and extrapolation fill gaps in coverage; they do not resolve overlap.

questions.question: An investor asks a maize project to report every farmer who received seed under the institutional adoption KPI, which counts farmers who planted it. What should the project do?

options.text: Adopt the investor's definition for the institutional KPI, since the investor funds the work
Rename the institutional KPI so that the two labels match in both reports
Pick whichever definition produces the higher number and use it for both
Keep the institutional definition and report the investor measure separately

questions.explanation: Projects may specify local scope but do not silently redefine the institutional indicator, so the investor measure is reported under its own definition with the difference recorded in the crosswalk. Matching labels does not make receipt and use the same thing.

questions.question: A project designs its own indicator for digital advisory uptake and labels it an institutional KPI on its dashboard. What does governance rule 1 say?

options.text: It stays project-specific until the Design, Standards & Enablement pillar has reviewed and approved it
Any indicator that uses a unit of observation from the Toolbox is automatically institutional
It becomes institutional once the investor accepts it in the indicator crosswalk
It becomes institutional after the Regional MEAL Lead signs off the measurement plan

questions.explanation: Projects can add project-specific indicators, but these are not reported as institutional KPIs until the Design, Standards & Enablement pillar has reviewed and approved them. A dashboard label, an investor agreement or a plan signature does not make an indicator institutional.

questions.question: A reference sheet requires direct measurement at farm level. A project proposes satellite yield estimates instead, arguing both give tons per hectare. How should a reviewer read the sheet?

options.text: Accept: the unit matches, so the method is valid for the KPI
Decline: the sheet sets valid methods, and satellite data serve calibration or upscaling under documented rules
Accept, but assign the satellite estimates the trial-level quality rating
Decline, because satellite data can never be used for any KPI at any level

questions.explanation: The reference sheet sets what is valid, and the triangulation rule says satellite or secondary data do not replace ground observations where the KPI method requires direct measurement; they are used for calibration, contextualisation, stratification or upscaling under documented rules. A matching unit is not a matching method.

Quality assurance and provenance
Calculation and aggregation rules

questions.question: A regional yield estimate for Kenya combines high-rated trial records and medium-rated farm records. How should its quality be reported?

As high, because the trial records carry controlled protocols
As medium, taking the lowest rating of any record in the set
Without a rating, since ratings stop mattering after aggregation

options.text: Because projects report their yields in different units and currencies
Because the sum is confidential until the annual KPI run is complete
Because contribution needs a counterfactual, modelling, adoption data and geospatial assessment
Because yield can only be measured credibly at trial stations

questions.question: Why does the framework insist that institutional values come from observation-level records rather than from project reports?

options.text: Because project reports usually arrive too late for the annual run
Because records keep provenance, so results can be recalculated, audited, disaggregated and reused
Because investors require the raw data attached to every submission
Because narrative reports cannot be stored in the MEAL data system

questions.explanation: The data system keeps the underlying records and their provenance so institutional results can be recalculated, audited and reused as methods improve, and direct observations permit disaggregation and re-analysis. Timing and storage are not the reason.

questions.question: A MEAL lead has only three project yield totals for Kenya and is asked what CIMMYT contributed to yield change there. What can she say honestly?

options.text: That CIMMYT raised yields by the sum of the three totals
That the average of the three totals is CIMMYT's contribution
That the highest of the three totals is the safest estimate
That the totals show what was reported, and the contribution question needs its own analysis

questions.explanation: Totals describe what projects reported; contribution needs analysis against a credible counterfactual with modelling, adoption and geospatial data built from observation-level records. Any arithmetic on the three totals dresses up a report count as a contribution claim.
